ELSEVIER Earth and Planetary Science Letters 150 ( 1997) 79-93 
Magnetic and sequence stratigraphy of redeposited Upper 
Cretaceous limestones in the Montagna della Maiella, Abruzzi, 
Italy 
S.A. Lampert a, W. Lowrie a- * , A.M. Hirt a, D. Bernoulli ‘, M. Mutti b.’ 
’ Institutfir Geophysik, ETH-Hikggerberg, 8093 Ziirich. Switzerland 
b Geologisches Institut, ETH-Zentrum. 8092 Ziirich. Switzerland 
Received 2 January 1997: revised 7 May 1997: accepted 7 May 1997 
Abstract 
The carbonate platform margin of the Montagna della Maiella in the Abruzzi region of central Italy has a complex history 
of sedimentation, consisting of aggradational and progradational episodes along the shelf margin and pelagic deposition in 
the basin. A paleomagnetic study at 12 regionally distributed limestone sites of late Cretaceous to Miocene age in the 
Maiella anticline was unable to define stable magnetic directions at most sites, largely due to the weakness of the 
magnetizations. At the few usable sites inclinations agreed with reference values based on an African polar wander path. 
Declinations were inconsistent, indicating local tectonic rotations. Both normal and reversed polarities were preserved at 
some sites. A magnetostratigraphic section, consisting of 280 samples spaced at l-l.5 m intervals, was sampled along a 
profile in the Valle delle Tre Grotte, near the village of Pennapiedimonte. Sequence stratigraphy, based on two-dimensional 
analysis of outcrops, formed the stratigraphic framework for the magnetostratigraphic study. Rock magnetic analyses showed 
that magnetite is the dominant ferromagnetic mineral in the limestones. Both alternating field and thermal demagnetization 
were satisfactory in defining two main components in the weak magnetizations. A component with low coercivity. low 
unblocking temperature and normal polarity was close in direction to the present axial dipole field direction at the site. A 
higher coercivity, higher unblocking temperature component with both polarities was interpreted as the characteristic 
remanent magnetization (ChRM). Although the mean directions of samples with normal and reversed polarity are not exactly 
antipodal. a stratigraphic sequence of magnetozones is very clearly defined. The Pennapiedimonte magnetostratigraphy 
correlates well with late Cretaceous Chrons C30r to C34n in the established polarity timescale; numerical ages can thus be 
allocated to the reversals. Correlation to the Gubbio section allows paleontological dates for the reversal sequence to be 
inferred. The correlations allow more precise dating of formational and sequence boundaries and a better evaluation of 
stratigraphic hiatuses. In particular, the boundary between the Tre Grotte Formation (Supersequence I, Turonian to middle 
Campanian) and the Orfento Formation (Supersequence 2, upper Campanian to upper Maastrichtian) is shown to be 
associated with a significant hiatus, spanning most of the middle Campanian G. uentricosa zone. Likewise. the absence of 
Chron C29r at the top of the Orfento Formation (SS2) documents non-deposition during the latest Maastrichtian or

subsequent erosion. Lower sedimentation rates in the Maastrichtian redeposited sediments than in the Gubbio section suggest

Keywords: paleomagnetism; limestone: Upper Cretaceous; Abruzzi Italy; tectonics; magnetostratigraphy: stratigraphy: correlation 
1. Introduction 
The Mesozoic and Cenozoic carbonate rocks of 
the Italian peninsula have proved to be a fertile 
ground for paleomagnetic investigations. Much of 
the sedimentary cover is allochthonous and only 
Apulia, together with the Gargano peninsula, the 
Iblean zone in Sicily, and small parts of the Southern 
Alps, are usually regarded as autochthonous. Paleo- 
magnetic data from the autochthons have an affinity 
with the African polar wander path [l] and are 
compatible with a tectonic model that ascribes these 
regions to an Adriatic promontory of the African 
plate [2,3]. Paleomagnetic directions of limestones in 
the dCcollement of the Umbria-Marche area are 
rotated counterclockwise relative to reference polar 
wander paths for both the African and European 
plates. At one time interpreted as paleomagnetic 
evidence for rotation of the Italian peninsula [4-61, 
the rotated paleomagnetic declinations evidently rep- 
resent rotations of the sedimentary cover [7.8]. Dif- 
ferential rotations affecting paleomagnetic vectors 
probably occurred during the emplacement of thrust 
sheets [9]. Deviations of tectonic elements and paleo-

Although a tectonic unit may have undergone

can be taken into account in evaluating magne-

stones of the Umbrian sequence in the Central Apen- 
nines have successfully established polarity se- 
quences that were dated in accompanying biostrati- 
graphic studies. These studies confirmed the record

82 S.A. Lampert et al./ Earth and Planetary Science Letters 150 (1997) 79-93 
of geomagnetic polarity derived from marine mag- 
netic anomalies and tied it to a paleontological 
framework from the Jurassic/Cretaceous boundary 
to the Eocene/Oligocene boundary [l 11. This makes 
it possible to use the magnetostratigraphy of a sec- 
tion as a first-order means of dating Paleogene and 
Cretaceous sediments with high resolution. 
In this paper we describe paleomagnetic studies in 
the Montagna della Maiella tectonic unit in eastern 
central Italy (Fig. 1). A regional paleomagnetic study 
was undertaken to complement the tectonic history 
of the region. A detailed magnetostratigraphic inves- 
tigation was made in a long continuous section in 
order to improve the dating of the basinal limestone 
sequence and to constrain better the duration of the 
stratigraphic hiatuses and the chronology of deposi- 
tional sequence boundaries. 
2. Geological setting 
The Maiella anticline is the frontal part of the 
most easterly allochthonous unit of the external 
Apennines in which Mesozoic and Tertiary sedi- 
ments are exposed (Figs. 1 and 2; [ 121). In the late 
Mesozoic to middle Tertiary the area was situated on 
the edge of a large, isolated carbonate platform, 
several hundred kilometres in size (the Apulian plat- 
form). The region developed on the southern margin 
SSE NNW 
Pesca Falcone Fm 
1 
1200 
of the Tethys ocean [ 131. Sedimentation began in the 
late Permian to late Triassic with the deposition of 
variable thicknesses of continental sediments and 
evaporites 1141. These include the Burano Anhydrite, 
which later served as a detachment horizon for over- 
thrusting during the Alpine orogeny [14]. Flooding 
by shallow seas in the latest Triassic to early Jurassic 
built up the carbonate megabank of the Calcare 
Massiccio Formation throughout the central and 
southern Apennines. This megabank disintegrated 
during early rifting in the ‘Liassic’, and a number of 
isolated, Bahamian-type carbonate platforms came 
into existence [15]. These long-lived carbonate plat- 
forms were separated by deeper basins, comparable 
to the present-day deep troughs of the Bahamian 
archipelago. They were the site of pelagic and - 
along the margins - turbiditic and other gravita- 
tional carbonate deposition, remote from terrigenous 
input [13,15]. During most of its early history, at 
least since the early Cretaceous and up to the late 
Campanian, the Maiella platform segment was bor- 
dered to the north by a steep, non-depositional es- 
carpment (Fig. 3) [ 16,171, which was most probably 
inherited from early Jurassic rifting but was shaped 
during its further evolution by submarine erosion and 
gravitational collapse. 
Towards the end of the early Cretaceous, the 
Apulian platform became emergent and was karsti- 
fied. In the Maiella, the exposed bank top was

re-flooded during the Cenomanian [16]. From the 
Cenomanian to late Campanian a 250 m thick suc- 
cession of peritidal cycles, bioclastic limestones, and 
rudist biostromes was deposited on the platform, 
whereas in the proximal basin a nearly 1000 m thick 
upper Cretaceous succession of pelagic/periplatform 
chalks and limestones, carbonate turbidites and 
megabreccias up to several tens of metres thick 
onlaps the escarpment (Inferno and Tre Grotte for- 
mations [I 81; Supersequence 1 of 1171). Because of 
the higher rate of aggradation in the basin, the 
deep-water sediments finally buried the escarpment. 
and shallower facies prograded over the former basin 
margins in the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian 
(Orfento Formation, Supersequence 2 of [I 7-201). 
From the latest Cretaceous to Oligocene, phases of 
subaerial and submarine erosion alternated with 
phases of prevailing platform aggradation and 
progradation along this platform margin [17]. A sec- 
ond progradation took place during the late Eocene 
(Priabonian) to Oligocene (Supersequence 5). It was 
preceded by a late Paleocene to middle Eocene 
interval of slope deposition and erosion (Superse- 
quences 3 and 4). In the late Oligocene and early 
Miocene the Maiella platform was deeply eroded. 
During the latest Oligocene to early Miocene a tem- 
perate carbonate shelf was established in the area 
(Supersequence 6). 
Extensive erosion under subaerial conditions took 
place during the Messinian, ending the evolution of 
carbonate platforms in central Italy. During the 
Miocene-Pliocene the carbonate platforms of the 
external Apennines were involved in thrusting and 
folding, resulting in stacked thrust sheets that strike 
mainly northwest-southeast and verge northeast [ 141. 
The surface expression of overthrusting in the Mon- 
tagna della Maiella is an anticlinal structure with an 
axis that has a shallow dip of less than 20” to the 
north [12]. It is bounded in the west by steep normal 
faults that set it off from the neighbouring Caraman- 
ice depression and in the east by a thrust that sepa- 
rates it from Pliocene deposits and allochthonous 
units of the Molise basin (Fig. 4). 
3. Regional paleomagnetic study 
Paleomagnetic samples were taken at 12 region- 
ally distributed sites in the Maiella anticline (Fig. 2). 
The rugged topography restricted access for paleo- 
magnetic sampling to sites along or near roads in the 
east and north of the region. At least ten cores, 
yielding 20-25 samples, were drilled at each site; a 
total of 255 samples was obtained for the study. The 
outcrops sampled ranged in age from late Cretaceous 
to Miocene and represent different lithologies and 
depositional environments. 
The magnetizations were measured with a 2G 
3-axis cryogenic magnetometer: the practical noise 
level of the instrument is equivalent to about 6 X 
10e6 A/m. Progressive thermal demagnetization and 
orthogonal vector diagrams [2l] were used to deter- 
mine the remanent magnetization components in each 
sample. Unfortunately, the intensity of natural rema- 
nent magnetization (NRM) was less than lop5 A/m 
in about 75% of the collection, so that the demagne-

### page_6
84 S.A. Lampert et al. /Earth and Planetary Science Letters 150 (1997) 79-93 
tized samples were mostly too weak to measure 
precisely. A reliable ChRM direction could be ex- 
tracted from only 33 samples at 4 sites in the Tre 
Grotte and Orfento formations. Two additional sites 
were formed of groups of 12 samples taken 100 m 
apart stratigraphically in the Pennapiedimonte mag- 
netostratigraphic section (described below). In some 
samples a magnetization component with northerly 
declination and positive inclination was removed 
below about 300°C (Fig. 5a). This normal polarity 
component masked a component with negative polar- 
ity that persisted up to 500-550°C which was taken 
as the ChRM direction. At some sites, after removal 
of a low blocking temperature component by 2OO”C, 
a ChRM with normal polarity was progressively 
demagnetized (Fig. 5b). 
Between 6 and 14 usable samples were obtained 
at each site. The site-mean ChRM directions and 
their statistical parameters [22] were computed after 
inverting reversed polarity samples (Table 1). The 
mean directions and their circles of confidence are 
plotted in Fig. 6. Sites MAO4 and MA08, with 
entirely normal polarities, overlap the current axial 
dipole field direction and may be remagnetized; they 
were excluded from further consideration. The incli- 
nations measured at the few acceptable sites are 
fairly consistent at around 40” (&- 5”), but the decli- 
nations show quite large variations (Fig. 2). 
Previous paleomagnetic studies on Cretaceous and 
Paleogene limestones in Central Italy have obtained 
evidence of tectonic rotations. Declinations at sites in 
the southwest Apennines showed evidence of both 
clockwise and counterclockwise rotations of al- 
lochthonous decollement nappes during thrusting 
[23,24]. In an earlier paleomagnetic-tectonic study

clockwise rotation of 24” (+ 15”) about a vertical 
axis. As in the present case, most of Jackson’s 
samples were unmeasurable. Moreover, the investi- 
gation was restricted to a very small area to the west 
of Fara San Martino, on the edge of the overthrust 
front (Fig. 21, and so the applicability of the result to 
the entire Maiella anticline is questionable. 
The recent compilation of paleomagnetic data by 
Van der Voo [26] was used as a basis for computing 
the reference directions for rocks of early Cretaceous 
to Miocene age at a location in the Maiella anticline 
(Table I). The inclinations observed at the Maiella 
sites are very similar to the reference inclinations. 
The declinations at sites MAO1 and P300 are not 
significantly different from the reference declina- 
tions; the declinations at sites MA03. P200 and the 
site of Jackson [25] are rotated clockwise relative to 
the reference values by different amounts. varying 
from 10” to 40”. This implies that Jackson’s direc- 
tions are a consequence of local rotation and are not 
representative of the Maiella crustal block as a whole. 
Despite the poor results obtained in the regional 
study, it is apparent that the upper Cretaceous rocks 
have good magnetic properties and carry both nor- 
mal and reversed polarities (Fig. 5). The partially 
resedimented upper Cretaceous limestones have not 
as yet been dated in enough detail for high-resolution 
stratigraphy. A magnetostratigraphic study was car- 
ried out with the goal of deriving a polarity se- 
quence, correlating it to the global magnetic polarity 
timescale, and thereby improving the dating of the 
depositional sequences recognized in these lime- 
stones [ I7,18].

4. Magnetostratigraphy of the Pennapiedimonte ity were taking place, may be due to later remagneti- 
section zation of the rocks. 
A great thickness of upper Cretaceous limestones 
(Supersequences 1 and 2, Fig. 3) is exposed in the 
canyon-like Valle delle Tre Grotte, which makes an 
east-west cut through the eastern flank of the Maiella 
anticline, to the west of the village of Pennapiedi- 
monte (Figs. 2 and 7). A magnetostratigraphic pro- 
file was made along a winding dirt road (part of the 
marked hiking trail No. 41, which provides better 
access to the head of the valley than an older path 
deeper in the canyon that it replaces. The strati- 
graphic framework for the sampling was provided by 
detailed studies of sequence stratigraphy in the 
Maiella that preceded our work [ 17-201. 
The sequence stratigraphy was developed from 
two-dimensional analysis of outcrops [181 and was 
documented by black and white photographic mon- 
tages. These were interpreted in the same way as 
seismic profiles and divided into individual se- 
quences of different order on the basis of combined 
geometric criteria and facies associations (Fig. 3). 
Supersequence (2nd-order) boundaries are pro- 
nounced truncation surfaces associated with signifi- 
cant chronostratigraphic hiatuses and a change in 
depositional system, whereas 3rd-order sequence 
boundaries reflect subaerial exposure of the platform 
and major events of redeposition in the basin [19]. 
The sequence stratigraphy was the key to under- 
standing the cycles of progradation and aggradation 
involved in the sedimentary evolution of the Maiella 
platform margin [ 17-201. 
The stratigraphically lower magnetostratigraphic 
profile was made through the upper part of Superse- 
quence 1 (Tre Grotte Formation, Turonian-middle 
Campanian) and through Supersequence 2 (Orfento 
Formation, upper Campanian-Maastrichtian). The 
profile contains truncation surfaces that indicate hia- 
tuses in deposition and submarine erosion. They are 
usually overlain by breccia or megabreccia beds that 
are several metres to tens of metres thick. Superse- 
quence 1 can be divided into two parts. The lower 
part consists of a 240 m thick succession of calcaren- 
ites and breccia, with an age estimated as middle to 
late Cenomanian [ 161. These sediments were not 
sampled. The upper part consists of a thick alterna- 
tion of upper Cretaceous pelagic limestones, rede- 
posited bioclastic sediments, and breccia containing 
clasts of platform carbonates. The base of Superse- 
Magnetizing Field bnTI 
In the Valle delle Tre Grotte Supersequences 3 
and 4 are reduced to local erosional relics, not 
present along the profile sampled, and Superse- 
quence 6 was not sampled. Two magnetostrati- 
graphic profiles were measured (Fig. 3). The strati- 
graphically higher profile was made in Superse- 
quence 5, which, on the basis of paleontological 
dating with large foraminifera, has a middle Eocene 
(earliest Bartonian stage) to early Oligocene (earliest 
Rupelian) age [ 181. It was not possible to obtain a 
polarity sequence in this profile. All 132 samples 
possessed only a single normal component of magne- 
tization; no reversed polarities were observed. The 
absence of magnetozones in these rocks, deposited at 
a time when frequent changes in geomagnetic polar-

quence 2 is a truncation surface with little relief, 
above which massive calcarenite beds were de- 
posited. The truncation is of late Campanian age and 
was thought not to represent a significant biostrati- 
graphic hiatus [16,18]. The top of Supersequence 2 is 
a truncation surface of regional significance. In our 
measured section it is overlain immediately by Su- 
persequence 5; the hiatus is here of late Maas- 
trichtian to mid-Eocene age [18]. The main Pen- 
napiedimonte magnetostratigraphic profile consisted 
of 241 samples of pelagic limestones and resedi- 
mented calcarenites representing a stratigraphic 
thickness of 340 m. The rapidly deposited megabrec- 
cias, up to tens of metres thick, were not sampled. 
The sampling interval in the pelagic limestones and 
calciturbidites averaged about 1.5 m in the lower 100 
m, and about 1 m in the upper 240 m of the profile. 
The indurated limestone offers little resistance to a 
diamond drill. This ‘softness’ and the white colour 
of the limestone raised initial doubts as to whether 
the ferromagnetic content would be suitable to allow 
the use of progressive demagnetization techniques. 
The ferromagnetic mineralogy of a number of 
samples spaced at wide intervals along the Pen- 
napiedimonte section was investigated with a method 
proposed by Lowrie [27]. The samples were first 
magnetized progressively until a saturation isother- 
mal remanent magnetization (IRM) was achieved. 
The IRM acquisition curves typically reached satura- 
tion in fields below 0.3 T, but in some samples a 
minor component persisted up to 0.6 T (Fig. 8). A 
field of 1 T was applied to produce saturation IRM 
along the axis of the cylindrical test samples. Next, a 
field of 0.6 T was used to produce a second IRM at

right angles to the first IRM. Finally, an IRM was 
produced in 0.15 T at right angles to both previous 
components. The composite IRM thus consisted of 
mutually orthogonal low ( < 0.15 T), medium (0.15- 
0.6 T) and high (0.6-l T) coercivity fractions. The 
thermal decay of each of these fractions was then 
studied during progressive thermal demagnetization 
(Fig. 8). The h’ h ig coercivity component was negligi- 
ble in all samples. The medium coercivity fraction 
was largely eliminated by 300-350°C. Both 
maghemite and pyrrhotite have maximum unblock- 
ing temperatures in this range. However, the persis- 
tence of a small fraction up to 0.6 T in some IRM 
acquisition curves suggests that a minor component 
may be carried by pyrrhotite. In all samples the low 
coercivity component was dominant; it was elimi- 
nated at temperatures in the range 530-580°C and is 
interpreted as being carried by magnetite. 
As in the regional study, the intensity of the NRM 
was very weak. However, approximately 75% of the 
samples collected were usable. Pilot studies carried 
out on twin specimens from the same drilled sample 
showed that both AF and thermal demagnetization 
could successfully define two components of rema- 
nent magnetization. The orthogonal vector diagrams

[2 I] show that peak alternating fields up to about 10 
mT or temperatures above 200-300°C are sufficient 
to remove an initial component with normal polarity. 
It overlies a more resistant component with normal 
(Fig. 9) or reversed (Fig. 10) polarity, which we 
interpret as the characteristic remanent magnetization 
(ChRM) direction of the sample. 
The low-coercivity, low blocking temperature, 
normal polarity component was clearly defined in a 
large number of samples. The directions of this 
component group lie around the direction of the 
present axial dipole field at the site (Fig. 11). We 
interpret it as a recent overprint, probably of viscous 
origin. 
The ChRM directions form two distinct groups, 
corresponding to normal and reversed polarities. The 
means of the respective groups are not exactly oppo- 
site (Fig. 12). The angle between the normal mean 
and the inverted reversed mean is 13.2”; each mean 
lies outside the circle of confidence of the other. The 
failure to pass the reversals test suggests incomplete 
removal of the secondary overprint. Each group con- 
tains many directions that deviate by large angles 
from the group mean. Despite the scatter, the ChRM 
polarity is unambiguous in each sample.

Pennapiedimonte evidently spans the sequence of 
polarity chrons from C3On to the top of C34n (the 
Cretaceous Polarity Superchron, or Quiet Interval). 
This allows the Pennapiedimonte section to be dated 
in absolute terms within the accuracy of the refer- 
ence timescale, by associating a numeric age with 
each polarity reversal. The correlation gives a mean 
sedimentation rate of 14 m/Ma in the Pennapiedi- 
monte section. This rate includes deposition of tur- 
bidites and other redeposited calcarenites and rudites, 
but it does not include the thick megabreccias below 
200 m (Fig. 15). 
5. Formational and sequence boundaries 
The Pennapiedimonte magnetostratigraphy also 
correlates well with magnetozones in the late Creta- 
ceous stratotype section in the Bottaccione gorge

inferred (Fig. 14b and Fig. 15), so that better dates 
can be associated with the supersequence (2nd-order) 
and sequence (3rd-order) boundaries. 
Supersequence boundaries are truncation surfaces 
that also separate different lithological formations, 
reflecting different depositional systems [ 17-201. In 
our section, the Supersequence boundary (SS l/SS2) 
separating the Tre Grotte from the Orfento Forma- 
tion was interpreted as being associated only with a 
minor hiatus within the Globotruncana (now 
Globotruncanita) calcarata zone [ 16,181. However, 
our data suggest a much longer duration. The

restricted to the uppermost few metres of the Tre

The base of the Orfento Formation is dated by 
Glohatruncana calcarata as late Campanian [ 181. 
The resulting hiatus, comprising most of the G. 
L>entricnsa zone, would also explain why Chron C33n 
(corresponding to zone B + in the Gubbio section) is 
thinner in the Pennapiedimonte section than in the 
generally thinner, distal Gubbio section, which does 
not contain calcareous turbidites (compare also Chron 
33r in the Pennapiedimonte section with zone A - 
in the Gubbio section, Fig. 14b). A correlation of the 
supersequence boundary SSI/SS2 with the base of 
cycle UZA 4.4 of Haq et al. [32] is compatible with 
our stratigraphic data (Fig. 15; cf. [ 18,201). If this is 
the case, the 3rd-order cycles UZA 4.1 to 4.3 are not 
represented in the Pennapiedimonte section. This is 
compatible with the progradation model of Mutti et 
al. [I 91. which suggests that, during times of aggra- 
dation, sediments were mainly trapped on shelf and 
marginal areas. However, pelagic sediments de- 
posited during UZA 4.1-4.3 must have been re- 
moved by erosion before deposition of sediments 
corresponding to UZA 4.4 (Orfento Formation). 
Supersequence SS2 (Orfento Formation) is over- 
lain along a pronounced truncation surface by relics 
of Supersequence 3/4 (lower Paleocene to middle 
Eocene) and Supersequence 5 (middle Eocene to 
lowermost Oligocene). As Chron C29r (zone G in 
the Gubbio section) is not present in the Pennapiedi- 
monte section, strata corresponding to the upper part 
of the late Maastrichtian Abathomphalus mayaroen- 
sis zone were not deposited or were eroded before 
deposition of the overlying Paleocene beds. This 
supersequence boundary might be correlated with the 
Supercycle boundary UZA 4/TA 1, which also falls 
in Chron C30n [32]. 
Lithoclastic megabreccias occurring in the Tre 
Grotte Formation have been interpreted as lowstand 
deposits overlying 3rd-order sequence boundaries 
[ 17,181. The megabreccia occurring near the top of 
Chron C34n f& in the Globntruncana (now Di- 
carinella) ccmcauata carinata or the Dicarimella 
asymmetrica zone, respectively. Its base could thus 
be correlated with the base of the 3rd-order cycle 
UZA 3.4 of Haq et al. [32], The younger UZA 
3.4/3.5 3rd-order cycle boundary is, however. not 
obvious from the stratigraphic record. 
Although almost entirely composed of redeposited 
lithologies. Supersequence 2 shows a lower mean 
sedimentation rate than the top part of Superse- 
quence 1 (Fig. 14a). Part of the section (Chron C3 1 r) 
is thicker than the corresponding E - interval of the 
more basinal Gubbio section, while another part 
(Chron C3 1 n) is thinner. This suggests that the record 
in the Pennapiedimonte section is punctuated by 
erosion (or at least non-deposition). Vecsei [IX] dis- 
tinguished four 3rd-order sequences in this superse- 
quence. One of these sequence boundaries (S 2.3/S 
2.4) at the base of the Globotruncana (now Gansse- 
rina) gansseri zone could correspond to the UZA 
4.4,WZA 4.5) boundary.

92 S.A. Lampert et al. / Earth and Planetary Science Letters 150 f 1997) 79-93 
6. Discussion Dl 
The paleomagnetic directions at the few usable 
sites in our regional study of the Montagna della 
Maiella have similar inclinations, which agree closely 
with expected values derived from reference data for 
the African plate. This is in agreement with other 
paleomagnetic observations in the Italian peninsula. 
The declinations at the usable sites showed quite 
large regional differences, which probably reflect 
local tectonic rotations. Considering the errors asso- 
ciated with both the reference data and our paleo- 
magnetic data, our results are compatible with tec- 
tonic displacements of the Maiella anticline docu- 
mented by seismic reflection results [33]. 
[31 
[41 
[51 
l61 
t71 
The upper Cretaceous limestones in the Montagna 
della Maiella record both polarities of the geomag- 
netic field. Magnetostratigraphy in the Pennapiedi- 
monte section agrees very well with the record of 
geomagnetic polarity in the late Cretaceous derived 
from marine magnetic anomalies. The numerical ages 
of Pennapiedimonte magnetozones can be obtained 
by correlation to the established polarity timescale. 
Alternatively, the anticipated levels of major paleon- 
tological zones can be obtained by correlation to the 
Gubbio section. The correlations provide stratigra- 
phers working in the Maiella with greatly improved 
dating of the resedimented sequence. For example, 
the ages of minor units within the stratigraphic su- 
persequences can be inferred. The study is an exam- 
ple of how magnetostratigraphy, under favourable 
circumstances, can provide a framework that permits 
more detailed basin analysis.
